It's Black Friday week and the Apple discounts keep on coming! If you're after a new MacBook, Apple Watch, iPad, or a different piece of Apple gear, then now is the best time to buy, as we're seeing some absolutely killer deals.
Take the always-in-demand MacBook Neo, which has received one of its first major discounts since the price rose to $699 earlier in the year. It's currently available for just $649 at Amazon. If you need a machine with a little more power, then there are also big savings to be had on various MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models.
Deals don't stick around forever, and some are selling out quickly, so act fast if you see something that you like here.
We'll be on hand all day today, November 25, to bring you the best Apple deals we can find, so keep checking back to see what's new.
iPhone 18 Pro: free w/ new line + unlimited @ T-Mobile T-Mobile is offering the iPhone 18 Pro for free when you open a new line and use three T-Mobile Picks. (T-Mobile's new data plans offer up to 3 Picks or free perks, such as DashPass by DoorDash or Netflix Standard. The number of Picks you get is based on the plan's price or how many phone lines are on your plan). In our iPhone 18 Pro review , we said it's the best phone money can buy. The iPhone 18 Pro features a 6.3-inch OLED 120Hz display (2622 x 1206), A20 Pro chipset, and 256GB of storage. You also get a 48MP main, 48MP ultrawide, 48MP telephoto lens w/ 4x zoom, and an 18MP front camera.
In our AirPods Pro 3 review, we said these earbuds are the best AirPods yet. With features like Live Translation, heart rate tracking, and integrated Siri, they're ideal if you want your earbuds to work for you. But if you "just" want industry-leading earbuds with perfect sound and great ANC, the Pro 3 won't let you down.
Price check: $149 @ Walmart | Sold out @ Amazon
Apple Watch Series 12 delivers the line's most accurate heart rate sensing yet, alongside a suite of advanced health and fitness features. It's powered by Apple's new S11 chip, which enables new Audio Intelligence features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap.
I didn't expect to see this deal. The new iPad mini A20 Pro is $100 off. The new model sports a larger 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR Display (2316 x 1512), A20 Pro CPU, 24% smaller bezels than its predecessor, and better audio. You also get a 12MP camera on the front and back and Wi-Fi 7 support. The base models (128GB/256GB) boast a 5-core CPU with 2 super cores and 3 efficiency cores, whereas the 512GB model bumps it to a 6-core CPU with 2 super cores and 4 efficiency cores. This is the first time it's on sale.
The Mac mini M6 keeps the ultra-compact 5x5-inch design introduced with the prior generation, but packs major performance upgrades under the hood. You get the raw speed of Apple's M6 chip, upgraded graphics with hardware-accelerated ray tracing for better 1080p gaming, 16GB of unified memory, and improved connectivity thanks to Apple's custom N1 chip, which adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread support.
If you're looking to save on your next iPhone, then AT&T has you covered. You can pick up the iPhone 18 Pro without paying a penny for the device. All you need to do is trade in an eligible device in good condition, and sign up for an AT&T Premium 2.0 plan or higher for three years.
You'll then receive monthly credits covering the cost of the phone, and means you only need to worry about covering the cost of the data plan itself. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is covered by a similar deal, though the increased cost means you do have to pay the extra $100 yourself.
iPhone 18 Pro: was $1,199 now $0 @ AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max: was $1,299 now $100 @ AT&T
If you're looking for a large-screen iPad, but don't want the expense of an iPad Pro, there's always the iPad Air. The latest lightweight Apple tablet comes powered by the M4 chipset, which offers excellent performance and energy efficiency — making this a machine that is capable, portable and long-lasting.
The iPad Air has also been discounted for Black Friday, letting you save on the latest Apple purchase.
iPad Air M4 (11-inch): was $749 now $649 @ Best Buy iPad Air M4 (13-inch): was $949 now $849 @ Best Buy
Need a new desktop machine? There are few better options than the latest Mac mini, which is powered by the latest M6 chip. This model comes with 16GB of RAM, a 256GB SSD and two rear USB-C ports. The M6 chip also offers improved graphics and computing power, with a healthy boost to AI processing at the same time.
All while offering the compact design the Mac mini lineup is known for — even if they aren't quite as compact as they were a couple of years ago.
Mac mini M6: was $899 now $799 @ Amazon
Apple has a reputation for making expensive products, which is why Black Friday deals are so important. It's one of the few times we get serious discounts on products like the Apple Studio Display, which just had $200 knocked off its $1,999 MSRP.
This 27-inch screen features a 5K Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, 60Hz refresh rate, two Thunderbolt 5 ports, an extra two standard USB-C ports, advanced speakers and microphones, as well as a tilt- and height-adjustable stand.
Apple Studio Display: was $1,999 now $1,799 @ Amazon
The iPad mini 8 might be brand new, but it's already been discounted thanks to Black Friday. In fact, Amazon has knocked $100 off the normal price, as long as you're happy with the Wi-Fi-only 128GB model that lacks the nano-texture display.
The new iPad also features a larger OLED display, the powerful A20 Pro chipset, excellent battery life, super-thin design, and excellent sound from the speakers. It also comes with some of the usual iPad mini features, including a 12MP camera, Wi-Fi 7, as well as IP67 water and dust resistance.
iPad mini 8: was $699 now $599 @ Amazon
If you've picked up an iPhone Duo, or you're waiting for it to arrive, you're going to want a stylus to go with it. The foldable supports the Apple Pencil USB-C, letting you draw and write by hand — instead of having to account for the imprecision of your fingers.
The good news is that the Apple Pencil is back to its lowest ever price, and it's not exclusive to the iPhone Duo. The stylus may not be as advanced as the Apple Pencil Pro, which is also on sale, but it does offer a basic option for every recently-released iPad.
Apple Pencil (USB-C): was $79 now $49 @ Amazon Apple Pencil Pro: was $129 now $99 @ Amazon
Apple makes a bunch of different wearables, but if you're looking for a basic option, the low cost Apple Watch SE 3 just got even cheaper ahead of Black Friday. It may not have the latest design, and it lacks some of the more advanced health features on other Apple Watches, but it's still excellent value — and available in much smaller sizes.
This is a wearable designed for health and fitness, with a range of different features to keep you healthy and active. Plus it runs the same software as more expensive Apple Watches, meaning your experience will be pretty similar — especially when you consider it has the same S10 processor as the Apple Watch 11.

articles.title_orig: Dow tumbles 700 points, Nasdaq loses 4% as Nvidia leads resumption of AI sell-off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow tumbles 700 points, Nasdaq loses 4% as Nvidia leads resumption of AI sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stocks fell sharply Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom. The moves largely erased the historic rally Monday that was sparked by Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO.
As of early Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 index was down more than 4%, the S&P 500 gave up nearly 3% and the Dow fell 900 points. Shares of Nvidia slid 7%.
The action marked a stark reversal from Monday, when financial markets staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025. The Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%.
Monday’s rally was primarily driven by Nvidia, one of the world’s largest AI chip design firms, which announced the surprise return of CEO Jensen Huang despite an ongoing scandal involving multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption.
But the good vibes didn’t last.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday.
“Clearly the latest declines have revived questions as to whether this selloff has further to run,” they said.
Before Monday’s rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory. The index fell further Wednesday into bear market territory, which is when an index falls 20% or more from its most recent high.
Shares of semiconductor and computer memory companies were the biggest drags Wednesday, along with Nvidia, down between 7% and 10% in early trading.
AI-related sentiment was damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week.
After a strong market debut Friday, with shares closing higher by more than 17%, Anthropic shares have been marred by three straight days of losses.
Anthropic’s shares are now about 10% below its IPO price, and almost 25% below where it closed on its first day, tumbling to $78 per share.
Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday.
Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold.
On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote.
On Wednesday, t he Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday.
That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months.
Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.”
“Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI.
Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal.
The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month.
A rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy for economists because it can indicate that high prices from energy costs are spilling over into the rest of the economy.
It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9.
Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical.
“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview . “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said.
A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs.
It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: US Targets China, EU With New Tariffs Citing Overcapacity
articles.title_zh: US Targets China, EU With New Tariffs Citing Overcapacity
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

articles.title_orig: A rising star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
articles.title_zh: A rising star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
articles.content_orig:
He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.
The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.
He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.
“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”
Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.
Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.
Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.
“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.
The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.
“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.
“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.
The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.
Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography .
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring .
The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest , a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.
The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.
Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.
“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.
Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.
Max Burman is deputy editor in the London bureau of NBC News Digital.

articles.title_zh: China's Hansoh Pharma strikes drug deal with Bayer unit worth nearly $3.3 billion
articles.content_orig:
China Southern Airlines said in a filing late Tuesday that its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines had agreed to purchase 50 Boeing 737-8 aircraft with a combined catalog price of approximately $7.4 billion.
The announcement comes after President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he expected China to purchase another 250 Boeing aircraft, following his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit last week.
"By the way, I sold 250 Boeings to China, and I think they're going to do another 250," Trump said.
In May, China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft for Chinese airlines following Trump's visit to Beijing, marking the country's first commitment to purchase U.S.-made Boeing aircraft since 2017, according to the White House.
It was not immediately clear whether Xiamen Airlines' latest purchase was part of that commitment.
China Southern, which owns a 55% stake in Xiamen Airlines, said the actual purchase price would be lower than the combined list price because of discounts offered by Boeing. The company did not disclose the final purchase price, citing confidentiality provisions in the agreement.
The aircraft are scheduled to be delivered in batches between 2031 and 2034, with the purchase financed through a combination of internal funds and external financing, the filing showed. The transaction remains subject to shareholder and relevant Chinese government approvals.
China Southern said the purchase would support Xiamen Airlines' planned relocation to the new Xiamen Xiang'an International Airport and the expansion of its route network.
The agreement follows the group's recent purchase agreement for 137 Airbus A320neo - family aircraft, the filing showed. China Southern said sourcing aircraft from different manufacturers would help diversify its fleet and improve operational flexibility.
Other Asian carriers, including Philippine Airlines and Malaysia Aviation Group , have also announced Boeing aircraft orders this month.

articles.title_orig: Poland Asks NATO to Shoot Down Russian Missiles Over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Poland Asks NATO to Shoot Down Russian Missiles Over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Fox News anchor Jon Scott reports on NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warning the alliance will defend every inch of Polish territory after a suspected airspace breach by Russia on ‘Fox Report.’
Poland announced Tuesday it had renewed its push for a permanent U.S. military presence in the country after two Russian airspace incursions in four days, including one in which a Swedish fighter jet under NATO command was cleared to shoot down a Russian cruise missile but held its fire.
The latest incursion came overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during attacks on Ukraine, four days after three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles had crossed into Poland, prompting NATO to scramble fighter jets and bolster air defenses along its eastern flank.
Poland's chargé d'affaires in Washington, Bogdan Klich, said Tuesday that he briefed the White House National Security Council on the violations and renewed Warsaw's call to permanently station American troops in the NATO member country.
US URGES AMERICANS IN HISTORIC REGION TO STAY ALERT AFTER 'DANGEROUS' AIRSPACE INCIDENT
"Yesterday, I briefed the U.S. National Security Council on the violation of Polish airspace by Russian Kh-101 missiles and once again discussed the issue of the permanent deployment of U.S. troops in Poland," Klich wrote on X .
The new diplomatic push follows the incidents involving Russian assets and heightened concerns that Moscow's war in Ukraine will spill into NATO territory .
The Nov. 20 incursion involved a Swedish JAS 39 Gripen pilot operating under NATO command who was authorized to engage a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, according to Lt. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, commander of Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, as reported by The Kyiv Independent .
NATO's Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany, issued conditional authorization to fire, but the pilot could not positively identify the object visually or through the aircraft's onboard electro-optical systems because of severe weather, Nowak said. No weapons were fired.
SUPERSONIC RUSSIAN JETS TRIGGER JOINT SCRAMBLE BY NATO ALLIES AMID PUTIN 'CLOWNS' JAB
Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters/File)
Polish authorities monitored 11 potentially threatening aerial objects during the attack, three of which entered the country's airspace, according to Nowak.
The Swedish Armed Forces said its jets had tracked several unidentified objects over Poland during the mission, which lasted several hours under difficult weather conditions.
Polish F-16 fighter jets, a Swedish Saab 340 early warning aircraft, a Dutch aerial refueling aircraft and ground-based air defense systems were also supporting the operation.
Polish prosecutors confirmed Sunday that debris recovered at three locations belonged to Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, revising an initial military assessment that one of the objects might have been a drone, according to reports .
RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS
His warning comes as NATO confronts a series of airspace violations, drone incidents and hybrid activity along its eastern flank. NATO’s military leadership said Friday that Russia’s actions continue to "test Allied resolve." (Olena Bartienieva/Getty Images)
Preliminary findings indicated the missiles were manufactured in October or November 2026 at a factory in Dubna in Russia's Moscow region, prosecutors said.
The second incursion happened overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine during another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Polish forces tracked the unmanned aircraft and received authorization to shoot it down but did not fire after it changed course and headed east, citing potential risks to civilians and property on the ground.
Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said Polish authorities believed the violation was deliberate.
"It's hard to imagine this being a coincidence, so we assume it was an intentional act," Zalewski told RMF FM, according to Reuters .
After an emergency meeting of the North Atlantic Council on Monday, Nov. 23, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe went on to authorize the forward deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to Poland .
NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski addresses a joint news conference at a meeting of the foreign ministers of the so-called Weimar Triangle of France, Germany and Poland with Ukraine's foreign minister in Warsaw Sept. 29, 2025 (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)
"All Allies stand in full solidarity with Poland. NATO remains united, ready, and committed to defending against any threat," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on X and as Warsaw summoned Russia's ambassador, according to Reuters.
In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said U.S. and Polish officials were working toward an agreement that could accommodate up to 10,000 American troops .
Roughly 7,000 U.S. troops were stationed in Poland on a rotational basis at the time while a permanent installation would expand Washington's military commitment along NATO's eastern flank.
"We want the kind of U.S. presence that would reassure us but not be threatening to Russia," Sikorski said during a Council on Foreign Relations event in New York, Bloomberg reported.

articles.title_orig: Migrant arrivals in Spain's Canary Islands break single-day record
articles.title_zh: Migrant arrivals in Spain's Canary Islands break single-day record
articles.content_orig:
Jörg Luyken is a Berlin-based journalist and writer of the German Review , a weekly newsletter on German current affairs
More than 2,000 migrants have reached the Canary Island of El Hierro, marking a new record for arrivals in a single day.
The Spanish coastguard recorded 2,121 migrants arriving aboard 15 boats on the tiny island on Tuesday. A four-day-old baby who was born during the voyage was among them, according to reports.
It is the latest indication that the perilous Atlantic crossing is becoming one of the main routes for illegal migration into Europe .
The figure breaks the previous daily record of 1,580 , set on Nov 14. The island has a population of 12,000 and is the second-smallest of the eight Canary Islands, at roughly 20 miles long and nine miles wide.
Many of the migrants set sail from Senegal in wooden fishing boats on a voyage of more than 800 nautical miles, which can take a week or longer.
Among those arriving on Tuesday was a deceased migrant, as well as about 100 children.
The crossing is among the deadliest of Europe’s irregular migration routes, with more than one in 20 migrants dying or disappearing at sea.
Fernando Clavijo, the Canary Islands’ regional leader, told Spanish radio station Cadena Ser: “Sadly, this is a historic day ... The sailing conditions were favourable and there was a full moon, so these people looking for a better future ended up on our shores.”
Five Spanish coastguard vessels are searching the waters around the islands for migrant boats. Those intercepted on Tuesday were escorted to port by rescue vessels before the occupants were distributed among three temporary reception centres on the islands.
Mr Clavijo warned that El Hierro could not cope with such a large influx. The reception centres are reportedly already overcrowded.
In recent years, arrivals along the West African route have fallen from 47,000 in 2024 to around 18,000 last year.
Although the route remained relatively quiet for much of this year, arrivals have increased in recent weeks. In October, Madrid declared a state of emergency in the Canary Islands, releasing additional funds to expand reception facilities.
The migration crisis is putting pressure on Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, before Sunday’s snap election.
In Ceuta , an estimated 10,000 migrants remain on the Spanish territory after tens of thousands surged across the border in July.
The events in Ceuta led to mass demonstrations in several Spanish cities over the government’s handling of the crisis.
Opposition politicians have accused Mr Sánchez of abandoning the people of Ceuta and of attempting to exonerate the Moroccan government for its alleged role in enabling the border crossings.
The prime minister is trailing the conservative Popular Party and hard-Right Vox in the polls, as voters lose faith in his party’s ability to control the situation in the country’s African and Atlantic territories.
During a campaign stop in Tenerife, Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, described the recent migrant arrivals as an “invasion”.

articles.title_orig: Another Hot Inflation Reading Keeps Fed on Track to Raise Rates Again
articles.title_zh: Another Hot Inflation Reading Keeps Fed on Track to Raise Rates Again
articles.content_orig:
Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.
The personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.
While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.
A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.
Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.
Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields also were sharply lower. Even with the higher-than-expected core inflation figure, expectations eased a bit for Fed rate hikes in 2027. Traders continued to price in two more increases but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch .
"Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.
The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. Less certain is how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years.
Inflation had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs also have continued to exert pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan.
Policymakers generally consider factors such as tariffs and supply shocks to be temporary, but some fear the impact has begun spreading through the economy and could become embedded.
"America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.
The large upward increase in GDP came from revisions to investment as well as consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of all economic activity, rose 4.2% in the third quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials regard as a key indicator of underlying demand, jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point.
In other economic news Wednesday, the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims slipped to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and back to around the lowest level since the late 1960s. Wall Street had been expecting 200,000.

articles.title_orig: Libyan naval officers die following Ukrainian drone attack, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Libyan naval officers die following Ukrainian drone attack, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Rather than peace, there is stark escalation.
That is the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US’ failed reframing of the process as about European security and participation.
Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone.
Russia launched Friday what Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year – a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv’s bridges, and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout.
Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times, in the days around the trilateral. And compounding that display of technical prowess, Kyiv’s drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad , and then Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast.
Where Moscow parades its brutal, relentless intensity, Kyiv strikes back with unexpected reach and precision.
The geography of Ukrainian strikes is important. Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland , hitherto considered safe – an odd legacy of the Soviet era, territory marooned in the heart of some of NATO’s most anti-Russian members.
The apparent strike against a Russian-linked military ship – the Sparta 2, one of their notorious military-cargo Sparta fleet – was likely by Ukraine, and either involved a drone launched from another ship, or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea. Inevitably Russia chose to blame a third option – that Lithuania permitted the drone to fly through its airspace – NATO territory. The accusation feeds the long-standing fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO. It also raises further the possibility of more Russian malfeasance and sabotage around the Baltics , and the risks of escalation with NATO this carries.
The Libya strikes – hitting a Russian naval ship and cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi, according to Zelensky – further showcases the ability of Kyiv’s drones to embarrass the Kremlin, which had over the last decade paraded its might in Africa, yet whose ships now bring great risk of damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they may dock.
The uptick in violence – and where it has spread – was unthinkable five years ago; from being contained inside Ukrainian territory, it spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO’s eastern borders, with Russia-linked sabotage across the military alliance. The frog is truly boiling, as this war is slowly spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons.
Firstly: the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, and everything from past conduct, to current funding – from Elon Musk to minor Pentagon officials – falls under their scrutiny, if not regulation. The peculiar sympathies with which Donald Trump acts in Russia’s favor will likely be reeled in, in sheer practical terms, and the focus of his inner coterie may turn more to survival under a looming Democratic White House, than their personal priorities when dealing with Putin’s war of choice.
What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
Moscow has palpably tried to set the negotiation clock backward, through persuading the US to reframe the talks as about wider “European security infrastructure.” This is something Moscow has long sought, a chance to rewrite the Ukraine conflict as the symptom of NATO’s enlargement eastward.
Putin himself has fortified his demands, his most recent appearance in Shenzhen stating Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire – the only real immediate deliverable for diplomacy now. Then he added if the Europeans wanted to join the talks on a technical level (as the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has said the Kremlin had consented to ) they should travel to Moscow to make the case to him, and then he’ll think about it.
Putin has clearly determined his best negotiating stance is to rip up what’s in front of him, step many paces back , and make any possibility of compromise seem remote.
There is a gruesome logic to this: reality is partially on Russia’s side on the battlefield. Capturing the remainder of the Donbas is openly Putin’s main war goal. And while Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying a Donbas town like Kostyantynivka for whole two years, neighboring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, as Russian drone and airstrikes force civilians out and streets into rubble, ready for the months of gruesome urban warfare ahead. Putin said in Shenzhen that Ukraine’s hold over this remaining 10% of Donbas may slowly become untenable. The horrific cost of Putin’s slow grind forwards, of at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, does come with some tiny results – almost absurd as they are, given the casualties.
Perhaps this is the short-term objective the Kremlin sees: make the remainder of Donbas rubble, and then accept a political settlement later, where you can claim victory over the ruins.
But it is the longer term danger that poses the greatest risk to diplomacy. Currently, few of the words spoken by either side relate to each other’s reality. European participation in future multilateral peace summits? Kushner says it’ll happen, the Kremlin says it won’t yet. Territorially, Putin says he controls Kostyantynivka, when he palpably does not. He said Thursday Ukraine started the war, when it did not.
Both sides’ demands seem to be moving away from each other. The Kremlin appears to want NATO to fall back and westward, according to some reporting. In turn, some reports suggest Ukraine’s membership of the alliance has even been floated by the US. These are two incompatible red lines.
The two sides’ parallel realities are getting further apart, rather than converging on a possible path forward. That is entirely Russia’s intention, and a textbook example of how they use diplomacy to advance their military objectives. But the impact is to create a fictional universe for diplomacy, in which a future restraint of reality on the battlefield becomes elusive. In short: you can’t expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing.
This is where the last year’s mess of failed talks, cosying up to Putin, belittling and bullying Ukraine, European panic and Russian savagery has led the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. A place where Ukrainian drones seem to hit anywhere there’s a Russian ship. Where Russian drones, missiles and helicopters stray monthly into NATO territory without fear of a military retaliation. And where the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace. It is a bleak moment whose only end in sight is the unsettling and even more destabilising collapse of either side.

articles.title_orig: How To Unlock Hurricane Weather In ‘GTA 6’
articles.title_zh: How To Unlock Hurricane Weather In ‘GTA 6’
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto 6 GTA 6 Rockstar Games
Grand Theft Auto 6 is a massive world filled with an incredible amount of detail and simulation. This includes the game’s dynamic and realistic weather system, a feature Rockstar hyped up quite a bit before launch. However, some players online aren’t seeing much rain and are claiming Rockstar lied. The reality is that, yes, rainstorms happen, but you might not be seeing them very often for a few reasons.
If you search around Reddit or Twitter , you’ll see a lot of people complaining that it never rains in GTA 6. However, you can also find amazing clips of thunderstorms pummeling Vice City. And I can confirm that when I played GTA 6 pre-release, I saw rainstorms and other weather events, like fog.  So what’s going on here? Why are some people suggesting the weather system in GTA 6 isn’t working or was a lie, while others, like myself, are dealing with thunderstorms?
THIS ISN'T JUST RAIN. THIS IS ENVIRONMENTAL ARTISTRY AT AN ABSURD LEVEL! 🤯
Just look at the rain dripping off the sides of the bridge, the incredibly atmospheric overcast skies and the way the entire scene comes together. GTA 6 genuinely looks like a work of art!
I'm quite… pic.twitter.com/NjbjmeYHV7
— VideoGameDetails (@VideoGameDetail) November 24, 2026
First up is that it does seem like something was borked with GTA 6 ‘s dynamic weather system at launch. On Monday, the first post-launch patch for GTA 6 arrived and fixed an issue that, according to Rockstar’s patch notes, led to the weather not changing for extended periods of time. So yeah, one reason it might not have been raining in your game is because of a bug.
However, even after the patch, some people are still claiming it isn’t raining in GTA 6 . And maybe something is still bugged. The more likely explanation is that people don’t realize just how dynamic and advanced the weather is in GTA 6.
In all previous Grand Theft Auto games and most other open-world games, when it rains in the game, it rains across the whole map. That’s not how weather in GTA 6 works. Instead, storms, fog, and other weather events can happen locally and in small parts of the map. At one point I was flying a plane and it was sunny, but ahead in the sky were big dark clouds. As I reached them, I entered a rainstorm. As I left the clouds behind, the rain stopped. So it’s very possible that it is raining somewhere in your GTA 6 world; you just aren’t in the spot where the rain is falling.
I’ve also seen some people suggesting the weather is locked to certain conditions earlier in the game, which seems plausible but hasn’t been confirmed by Rockstar yet. Once I reached chapter three of the game, I had a few in-game days when it rained a lot. I started to miss the sun.
The point is that, no, Rockstar didn’t lie. Grand Theft Auto 6 ‘s dynamic weather system is so good that I think some people are just dodging the rain without realizing it. The size of the map and the randomness at play in the system may mean that you go for a while without encountering rainy weather, but keep playing and sooner or later, the storms will come.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
articles.content_orig:
The party of Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing party in a bid to form the next government following October’s elections .
The centrist Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
After no bloc managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming ⁠a government, while Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping him of his majority.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
The right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority, which hold 19 seats and ⁠are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.
The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with the Arab parties.

articles.title_orig: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war, new estimate suggests
articles.title_zh: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war, new estimate suggests
articles.content_orig:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine , according to a new projection based on leaked official data, an estimate that sheds new light on the staggering cost of President Vladimir Putin ’s war.
The grim assessment comes more than 4½ years after the Kremlin’s invasion of its neighbor, an all-out war that has consumed Russian society . The death toll has been mounting with each painstaking ground assault, with no end to the conflict in sight despite pressure from President Donald Trump for Kyiv to make a deal.
The leak from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat — released by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers earlier this month — reveals that at least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in Ukraine based on registered deaths as of the end of September. That’s according to breakdowns by a range of independent media, including the BBC and others, that were published this week. But one exiled Russian media outlet, Meduza, also used the leaked mortality data to project the total number of military deaths, including those that have not yet been recorded.
Meduza estimates that number to be 720,000.
NBC News did not have access to the leaked data and could not authenticate it or independently confirm these numbers.
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv provide regular updates on their battlefield losses.
Mediazona, along with the BBC Russian Service and a team of volunteers, has been compiling a separate named list of Russian war dead using open-source data for years, given the difficulty of gauging the true impact of the war on Russian society.
In its analysis, Mediazona said it arrived at the 490,000 war dead number from the 29.7 million records it obtained from the hackers that covered nearly all death registrations in Russia from early 2021 through September this year, based mainly on records with an “explicit military cause of death” and court rulings declaring people dead.
The leaked data was cross-checked against Mediazona’s own named list and matched 95% of the records, as well as the publicly accessible national Probate Registry, a database of inheritance cases, and Rosstat’s own official mortality statistics, the outlet said.
Mediazona said it also checked against possible data tempering and fake military death injections by cross-referencing a unique vital record number that every death registration carries, and court rulings, which often cite death record numbers.
“We are confident that this data is genuine,” the outlet said, adding that fabricating a dataset of this scale from scratch would be “impossible” especially as it checks out against official registries.
The hackers shared leaked data with a number of other exiled Russian media outlets and the BBC, who all arrived at a figure close to the 490,000 reported by Mediazona. A similar estimate of half a million Russian troops killed was also shared by a senior British defense official in September.
Before the new analysis of the data in the Rosstat leak, the verified named list of Russia’s war dead compiled by Mediazona and the BBC stood at just over 289,000. It was based on obituaries, local news and official registries, and was the only publicly available database containing the fallen soldiers’ names.
The Russian Defense Ministry has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early months of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said it stood at nearly 6,000.
Mediazona warned that due to a considerable lag in military death registrations, Rosstat may not yet have finished capturing deaths from 2025. “That means the leaked records through late September — however authentic and reliable they are — still fall short of the true death toll,” it said.
It was this that prompted Meduza to try and calculate an estimate of total Russian losses to date — 720,000 people, a figure that includes deaths it predicts will be registered later.
“Since 2024, the share of late registrations has grown dramatically, and it continues to rise,” the outlet said in its own analysis, adding that the 2026 data is extremely incomplete for both missing service members and other military deaths. It said it used epidemiology and tools like the “chain-ladder method” from actuarial science, which uses mathematics to help measure the probability and risk of future events, to arrive at the projected estimate. These methods allowed Meduza to calculate the number of military deaths that it estimates have happened but haven’t yet shown up in the data, the outlet said.
“Today, it’s simply impossible to leave this category out of an overall estimate of the dead,” it added.
The Kremlin dismissed the analysis Wednesday.
“The only department authorized to officially release data on casualties is the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told NBC News during a call with reporters, when asked if the Kremlin was aware of the 700,000 projected estimate by Meduza.
“I suggest disregarding any other data,” he added.
It is similarly difficult to ascertain the true number of Ukrainian soldiers killed fighting against Russia. Kyiv has been slightly more forthcoming, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy volunteering some estimates of battlefield losses in recent years, the latest in July putting the total at around 50,000 killed.
But analysts say this is likely an undercount.
An assessment by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies earlier this year said up to 150,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed, based on estimates from Britain’s military, Mediazona’s named war dead list, its own estimates and interviews with U.S., European, Ukrainian and other government officials.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.title_zh: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll , a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .
Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.
The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

articles.title_orig: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
articles.title_zh: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
articles.content_orig:
As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions.
Because of high gas prices , the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird.
"Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much."
With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season . At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate.
Some are raiding their savings accounts and running up debt on credit cards. They're reporting downbeat outlooks about the economy in surveys. And they've become more selective with spending as inflationary pressures mount.
"Families are facing some tough choices this year," said Alexander Smith, an associate professor who researches behavioral economics at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute. "They might have to cut back on holiday spending in whatever way that they can."
A classic Thanksgiving feast will be harder to pull off as grocery prices rise.
The price of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased 6% to $58.63 in 2026, according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. Faith Parum, the organization's deputy chief economist, said the price increase was a result of higher costs for labor and transportation.
Grocers including Walmart and Aldi have gained traction on social media by offering Thanksgiving meal bundles as a value-focused workaround to higher prices. Walmart's offering promises to feed 10 for $35, and includes a turkey and ingredients to make mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, cranberries, marshmallow-topped sweet potatoes and a pumpkin pie.
Still, some consumers will feel disappointed by having less choice in their menus due to higher prices, according to Joe Bruseulas, chief economist at tax firm RSM.
"We're missing the point here if all we're doing is focusing on the fact that Walmart will sell you a homogeneous dinner meal" at a discount, Bruseulas said. "People feel horrible that they have to go to that because the price of everything has just risen so significantly over the past five years."
Inflation is affecting more than Thanksgiving staples like turkey or stuffing. Food prices on average have jumped around 24% over the last five years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Some items have seen even sharper increases: Coffee and ground beef, for example, have each climbed by more than 40% in the same period despite pulling back from recent highs.
At the same time, millions of Americans lost SNAP benefits under policy changes included in President Donald Trump 's "big beautiful bill." Food banks across the U.S. have seen foot traffic skyrocket this year as the reduction in federal nutrition aid coincides with rising prices in grocery aisles.
The Salvation Army said some of its food pantries in October provided double or triple the amount of groceries than they did in the same month a year ago. Demand is now so high that some food banks in Feeding America's national network are worried about running out of supplies.
"We want to make sure that our food banks are as full as they possibly can be going into the holiday season," said Linda Nageotte, Feeding America's president and operations chief. "Far too many of them have empty shelves."
High energy prices as a result of the war with Iran are also affecting Americans' holiday plans.
Slightly fewer Americans will travel at least 50 miles around the Thanksgiving holiday in 2026, marking the first year-over-year decline since the country was in lockdown from the pandemic in 2020, according to AAA. Stacey Barber, a vice president at the auto association, attributed this year's pullback in part to higher fuel costs.
AAA said that about nine out of every 10 Thanksgiving travelers will do so by car. While gas prices have come down from a May peak, they are still up about 18% year over year and could set a new record for the month of November, according to the organization's data.
Travelers are paying about 31% and 23% more for roundtrip domestic airfare around Thanksgiving and Christmas, respectively, than they did a year ago, according to booking platform Hopper. Airlines have blamed the ticket price hikes on rising jet fuel costs in the wake of the war.
"There will be a significant shell shock when they see the price of traveling," said Hayley Berg, lead economist at Hopper.
Berg said price increases would feel more noticeable on routes previously serviced by Spirit, the budget airline that shut down in May. Travelers are booking holiday flights earlier than they did in past years, a sign that prices are top of mind, she said.
Staying home for the holidays isn't a silver-bullet solution, either, as heating costs jump.
The average American household is expected to spend 7% more on home heating this winter than they did last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. For the typical family, that equates to an increase of about $66 and a total bill for the season above $1,000.
To be sure, some families will feel it more than others. Heating oil , which is used mainly in homes in the Northeast, has jumped around 70% year over year. However, natural gas , which is one of the most common heating types in the U.S., costs about the same as last year.
Some U.S. states, like Massachusetts and New York, beefed up their home energy support programs to account for higher prices. But Mark Wolfe, NEADA's executive director, said federal aid offerings haven't been meaningfully expanded this year.
"Some of these increases are caused directly by the decision to go to war," Wolfe said. "Why isn't the federal government helping families pay these higher bills?"
The spirit of giving will take on a different meaning for consumers this year.
Retail sales during the all-important holiday season are expected to grow almost 5% this year and surpass $1 trillion for the first time , according to Bain & Company. But the consulting firm said most of that growth would come from inflation, rather than from consumers buying more products.
And Citi on Wednesday said that increased holiday spending would be mainly driven by higher earners this year. The bank said that's a result of the "K"-shaped economy , a term used to describe a scenario where better-off Americans splash out while others struggle.
Toy prices have climbed more than 9% over the past year and now sit at their highest levels since 2019, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Manufacturers have raised prices in response to higher costs for transportation and plastic , according to Chris Byrne, an independent toy industry analyst. The artificial intelligence boom has driven up prices for the chips that power gaming devices and other electronics.
Byrne said that's causing shoppers to focus more on the quality of gifts rather than quantity.
"The toy industry always reflects the culture at large," Byrne said. "It's almost true economically as well. As inflation is rising, people are being a little bit more cautious about what they're buying."
Just 16% of respondents to a Morning Consult survey said they planned to spend more in the 2026 holiday season than they did a year ago. Respondents who were older or had lower earnings were more likely to say their budgets were shrinking, the survey found.
Some are doing away with gifts altogether. A poll from consulting firm TSG and the Electronic Transactions Association found 5% of Americans did not plan to buy any presents in 2026, up three percentage points from l

articles.title_orig: Acer Predator Atlas 8 Review: Potent Performance At A Slightly Better Price
articles.title_zh: Acer Predator Atlas 8 Review: Potent Performance At A Slightly Better Price
articles.content_orig:
Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival.
Modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home. But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance. This culminated most recently in systems like MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+ , which delivers serious graphics power along with an equally serious price of $1,800. But now, Acer is trying to undercut the current framerate champ with the Predator Atlas 8, equipping it with the exact same chip used in MSI's machine, but for $350 less. The result is a compelling package that delivers on many of the same highs while easing the burden on your wallet.
With the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs. The middle of the system is dominated by a large 8-inch LCD TFT display with a 120Hz refresh and respectable 500-nit brightness. On the outside you get TMR analog sticks along with an Xbox-style button layout. I must admit I'm not a huge fan of Acer's circular D-Pad as it's a bit mushy and doesn't feel super precise. But if you're not playing fighting games or similar titles, it's more than serviceable for navigating menus. And if I'm really nitpicking, colors from the Predator's TFT screen aren't quite as rich as what you get from MSI's machine, but it's the kind of difference that you only really notice when you look at the two systems side by side.
Around back, Acer included a pair of rear paddles, two shoulder buttons and analog Hall-effect triggers with plenty of travel — the latter of which are great for racing games. Along the top edge of the system you get all of the Predator Atlas 8's ports, which includes dual USB-C jacks with support for Thunderbolt 4, a microSD card reader for expandable storage, a 3.5mm audio jack and a power button with a built-in fingerprint reader.
All told, it's a pretty standard setup, though the Predator does lack a USB-A port like you get on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. I also noticed that while Acer's dual two-watt speakers can get surprisingly loud, audio becomes distorted at higher volumes (above 50 TK) that results in a crackly or crunchy sound. That said, the speakers are so punchy, I found that I never really needed to turn them up that high. Unless you're trying to DJ a house party with this thing, you might not even notice.
The real star of the Atlas 8 is its Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which is the exact same chip used in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The main difference is that Acer's handheld comes with 512GB of storage instead of 1TB and tops out with 24GB of shared memory (compared to 32GB on the MSI). This discrepancy almost entirely accounts for the price gap between the two systems. But for people striving for top-notch performance while trying to save a few bucks, the framerate delta in games isn't as pronounced as you might think.
When I tested this out in Cyberpunk 2077 at 35 watts on FHD, medium graphics and XeSS set to performance, the Predator Atlas 8 hit 88 fps, which is barely more than five percent lower than the 95 fps I got from the Claw 8 EX AI+. But it's important to note that this was using Acer's highest performance mode. When I set the system to 15 watts (which you might do when playing on battery only), the Predator and the Claw were essentially dead even in Returnal at FHD and medium graphics (60 fps for the Acer vs 59 fps for the MSI). This means that if you're trying to decide between the two, you really need to consider how you plan on using your handheld and what types of games you'll be playing.
Similar to other high-end Windows handhelds, the Atlas 8 comes with Microsoft's Xbox experience. This software allows you to boot into a dedicated UI for gaming instead of needing to deal with the traditional desktop OS. This also makes it super easy to download all of the most popular launchers and storefronts like Epic, Steam, Battle.net and more, and because it's Windows underneath, you get better compatibility than what you get from SteamOS-powered portables. That said, if you're the type to travel with a portable monitor, keyboard and mouse, you can still switch over to the classic Windows interface to get some work done too.
The Atlas 8 is powered by an 80WHr battery that provides ample longevity, though it can vary quite a bit depending on what you're playing. However, without even doing anything to boost its longevity, I was able to play World of Warcraft: Forever at FHD on medium settings for an hour and 45 minutes on a single charge while still keeping frame rates consistently above 90. On the flipside, when I played a less demanding title like Warhammer Survivors, Acer's machine had more battery life than I knew what to do with: It lasted for more than three hours before needing to be plugged in. Notably, both of those games were played using the handheld's 30-watt Balanced performance mode, so if you're not afraid to mess around with its settings, there's a lot of room to tweak this thing to get even longer untethered gaming sessions.
I'm still not sure how I feel about PC handhelds that cost well above $1,000. For me, that's just a ton of money to drop on a system that can't multitask as well as a similarly priced gaming laptop. However, for mobile gaming enthusiasts trying to find the sweet spot between price, performance and portability, Acer has carved out an interesting niche with the Predator Atlas 8.
At $1,450, it costs $350 less than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, while sporting the exact same processor and delivering essentially 95 percent of the performance. That said, Acer's more approachable pricing leaves the Predator with a bit less RAM and storage, though having a microSD card slot provides a workaround for the latter. There are also some minor differences, like the lack of a USB-A port, a slightly less colorful TFT display and speakers that sound a bit wonky at high volumes. But these shortcomings could very well be a worthwhile trade-off for anyone looking for peak handheld gaming performance without completely fragging their budget.
