articles.title_orig: Ukraine Says 3 MiG-31s, 2 Su-34s Hit at Russian Airfield, 2 Refineries Damaged
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Says 3 MiG-31s, 2 Su-34s Hit at Russian Airfield, 2 Refineries Damaged
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed that three MiG-31 fighter jets and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were hit at Russia’s Savasleyka military airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region. The defense ministry also detailed damage to processing units and storage tanks at the Kuibyshev and Syzran oil refineries in the Samara region, both owned by Rosneft.
Ukraine’s military has detailed the damage inflicted on two major Russian oil refineries in the Samara Oblast and confirmed that five aircraft were hit at the Savasleyka military airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region during overnight strikes on Wednesday, Nov. 25.
The strikes were reported earlier by Kyiv Post . Ukraine’s General Staff and defense ministry have now released details of the damage.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
At the Kuibyshev Oil Refinery, Ukrainian forces struck the AVT-4 and AVT-5 primary oil processing units, a catalytic reforming unit and two storage tanks. A fire broke out at the facility, the defense ministry said.
At the Syzran Oil Refinery, preliminary assessments indicate damage to primary oil processing, sulfur treatment, catalytic reforming, hydrotreating and isomerization units, as well as two storage tanks. A large-scale fire also broke out at the plant.
Both refineries belong to Russian oil giant Rosneft and have a combined annual processing capacity of more than 15 million metric tons (16.5 million US tons) of crude oil.
The defense ministry said the Syzran refinery had been targeted at least 10 times since August 2025, while the Kuibyshev facility had been struck five times.
Both plants suspended operations following Ukrainian strikes in September 2026 and underwent two months of repairs, according to the ministry.
The overnight attack comes amid an escalating Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s oil infrastructure.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces have struck 16 Russian refineries since the beginning of November, forcing some to suspend operations and others to reduce production.
Russian oil refining volumes fell by 45% during the first three weeks of November, according to industry sources cited by Reuters .
With much of Russia’s western refining infrastructure repeatedly coming under attack, President Vladimir Putin has called on oil companies to expand refining capacity in Siberia and the Far East.
Ukraine’s military also provided details of the strike on Savasleyka, a Russian military airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region that hosts MiG-31K aircraft capable of carrying Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles.
Russia regularly uses the missiles to attack Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
According to preliminary information from the General Staff, three MiG-31 aircraft and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were hit during the operation.
The General Staff said the damaged aircraft would be unable to fly for “a certain period.” The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The airfield has been targeted by Ukrainian forces in several previous operations.
In August 2024, Ukrainian military intelligence drones attacked Savasleyka twice. A Kyiv Post report , citing a source in Ukrainian intelligence, said the Aug. 13 strike hit a fuel and lubricant depot and damaged a MiG-31K/I.
A subsequent attack on Aug. 16 destroyed a MiG-31K/I and two Il-76 transport aircraft, while damaging about five other aircraft, believed to include MiG-31s, the source said.
Ukraine struck the airfield again on June 9, 2025. The General Staff confirmed the operation , saying two Russian aircraft had been hit. Preliminary information indicated they were a MiG-31 and either a Su-30 or Su-34.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Inside the Scramble to Avert Conflict With Russia in the Baltic
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Inside the Scramble to Avert Conflict With Russia in the Baltic
articles.content_orig:
President of Finland Alexander Stubb and the Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Støre called the Russian dictator To Vladimir Putin ...on October 27 to reassure him that NATO countries do not plan to blockade the Baltic Sea, through which Russia exports the majority of its oil by sea. As... found out According to The Wall Street Journal, European leaders feared a military confrontation with Russia over the situation surrounding its shadow fleet, even though the main topic of the call was officially ending the war in Ukraine.
Stubb and Støre wanted to assure Putin that NATO countries do not intend to block Russia's oil export route through the Baltic Sea.
"We have no intention of blocking the Baltic Sea in peacetime. You can count on that; we will act in accordance with the law," Stubb told Putin, according to two people present during the conversation.
The rise in tension was caused by attempts by European countries to stop and inspect tankers belonging to Russia's "shadow fleet," which Moscow uses to circumvent oil sanctions.
According to WSJ estimates, such tankers have been detained or inspected at least 14 times since late 2024. Ten of these incidents occurred in early 2026.
In response, Russia began using warships armed with nuclear-capable missiles to escort its tankers. Over a period of just over a year, the German Coast Guard recorded 260 such escorts in the Baltic and North Seas. Eventually, operations to intercept tankers in the Baltic all but ceased.
More than 60% of the oil Russia exports by sea passes through the Baltic Sea. European countries have sought to limit these exports in order to reduce revenues. from oil sales and finance the war against Ukraine .
According to the WSJ, Western officials were concerned about several decisions made by Moscow:
→ In May 2026, Russia adopted legislation authorizing the use of military force to protect merchant vessels.
→ Russia has deployed drones, powerful radars, and electronic warfare systems to the Kaliningrad region, located between Poland and Lithuania.
→ In August, Putin called European countries' attempts to stop Russian tankers "piracy and banditry" and threatened a military response.
In September, the Kremlin sent NATO a written warning regarding its readiness to launch preemptive nuclear strikes to protect its interests in the Baltic Sea, even if no one were to attack Russian territory.

articles.title_orig: Europe plans €50 billion sovereign tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
articles.title_zh: Europe plans €50 billion sovereign tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
articles.content_orig:
In September 2017, Google researcher Austin Fowler stood before a room of quantum engineers at a conference in College Park, Md., and admitted something rarely heard from Big Tech: He was stuck. Quantum computers make mistakes constantly, and every error must be caught within a millionth of a second before the whole calculation collapses. The best chip available was still 10 times too slow, Fowler said. Many in the room left convinced the problem might never be solved.
But across the Atlantic, on a quiet street in Cambridge, a five-person startup was developing its own solution to the problem. Steve Brierley, a Cambridge University research fellow, had founded Riverlane from his kitchen table the year before. “Even Google can’t solve this problem,” he recalls thinking when he heard Fowler’s admission. In 2024, Riverlane ran what it describes as the world’s first low-latency quantum error-correction experiment, decoding errors in under a microsecond— fast enough to keep the machine running.
Today, Riverlane employs nearly 200 people and works with more than 60% of the world’s quantum computer makers.
With U.S. tech companies dominating the digital economy, and China and America pulling ahead in the race for AI supremacy, quantum computing represents a rare opportunity for Europe to establish itself at the forefront of a transformative technology. The European Commission’s Quantum Europe Strategy, aims to make the continent a global quantum leader by 2030, and McKinsey estimates the technology could create $2.7 trillion of economic value worldwide by 2035.
The most advanced quantum computers hang like gilded chandeliers, their cores chilled to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero, more than 100 times as cold as deep space. Quantum technology builds on the principles of quantum mechanics and the ability of particles to act as both a particle and wave. Quantum computers harness this capability with qubits, allowing them to tackle problems that are prohibitively difficult for conventional machines, such as simulating molecules to accelerate drug discovery or modeling complex financial risks.
Development of a quantum computer that is sufficiently powerful and reliable to complete these tasks would have strategic implications for nations, as it would theoretically be capable of breaking the encryption protecting banks and digital communications.
“The company that builds the first large-scale quantum machine could seize an entire industry overnight,” says Jérémie Guillaud, an architect at Alice & Bob, one of France’s most promising quantum startups. Guillaud believes that the winner could be European. “There is a good possibility.”
“We haven’t lost the race yet,” says Lionel ­ Martellini, a finance professor with a PhD in astrophysics who founded the EDHEC Quantum Institute in France. “Which doesn’t mean that we’re not going to lose it.”
Quantum was “born in Europe,” Martellini notes, and the continent still produces much of the field’s foundational research. Quantum theory grew out of the work of Max Planck, Niels Bohr, Albert Einstein, Erwin Schrödinger, and Werner Heisenberg in the early 20th century. European physicists have since collected a string of quantum Nobel prizes.
Source: McKinsey: The Joint Research Centre
That legacy has seeded a thriving startup scene. The EU is home to 32% of the world’s quantum technology companies, according to the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre.
France alone has five leading hardware contenders—Pasqal, Alice & Bob, Quandela, Quobly, and C12—each developing a different way to build a qubit, the basic unit of a quantum computer. Britain has Oxford Quantum Circuits and Riverlane, and Finland’s IQM says it has sold 26 quantum computers for customers to install on-site, the most publicly disclosed by any manufacturer.
“Europe has a tremendous opportunity with quantum,” says Ana Paula Assis, senior vice president and chair for IBM Europe, Middle East, Africa, and Asia Pacific. “The region’s diverse industrial base holds both the prob- lems quantum computers are built to solve and the data needed to solve them,” she says.
That has made Europe the industry’s biggest customer base. Two-fifths (43%) of quantum computing companies’ customers are headquartered on the continent, according to McKinsey’s Quantum Technology Monitor 2026. Much of that demand comes from public supercomputing centers, which allow researchers and companies to rent machines from European makers such as IQM and Pasqal.
European nations have committed $15.9 billion to quantum technologies in the five years to 2025. U.S. federal funding had reached only about $6 billion until May, when Washington pledged a further $2 billion to nine quantum companies.
However, private investment in quantum startups is still dominated by the U.S. A record $12.6 billion was invested worldwide in 2025, more than six times the 2024 total, with 64% going to American companies, according to McKinsey. The European Commission estimates that European quantum firms attract only about 5% of global private funding.
“American startups can draw on pension funds and university endowments, but there is no real European equivalent. We don’t have a unified marketplace, and we don’t have a very strong pension system,” Martellini says.
“In France we have ideas, but no money,” says Alice & Bob’s Guillaud. “We won’t build a useful quantum computer just using ideas.” Alice & Bob’s €100 million ($110 million) Series B, one of Europe’s larger quantum rounds, is dwarfed by the $1 billion the California company PsiQuantum raised in a single round in September 2025.
Consequently, many of Europe’s brightest prospects have crossed the Atlantic for capital. Britain’s Oxford Ionics was sold to U.S.-listed IonQ for $1.075 billion in 2025, and this year Finland’s IQM and France’s Pasqal both floated on Nasdaq. IQM also trades in Helsinki, and Pasqal is planning a second listing in Paris.
Wasiq Bokhari, Pasqal’s chief executive, insists it was never a choice between New York and Paris. “Nasdaq just happened to be our first public listing on the way to our eventual Euronext listing,” he says. “Once a quantum company reaches the commercial stage it’s important to get access to capital at scale.”
The bigger problem, according to Bokhari, is Europe’s scattered funding model, which is split across national plans.
“The U.S. and China are single entities able to make decisions quickly,” Bokhari says. “Europe has all the ingredients. We just need to make sure we align them quickly and in a unified direction.” The EU’s Quantum Act, which aims to coordinate research and spending across the bloc, could help.
The frontier, meanwhile, is racing ahead. The most powerful quantum computers remain in the U.S. and China, led by IBM, Google, Quantinuum, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences. IBM is building its first large- scale, error-corrected machine in Poughkeepsie, N.Y., which will be capable of running 20,000 times as many operations as today’s machines.
Alessandro Curioni, vice president of IBM Research Europe and Africa, says this puts the company “two to five years ahead” of the pack on top-class hardware. That, he argues, means Europe risks “running the wrong race.” In his view, “the real prize is not the machines but a new software industry combining AI and quantum computing.” Europe’s diverse industrial economy gives it the best shot at leading that industry, he says, “but only if it starts now, on whatever machines are best.”
“Europe has all the ingredients. We just need to make sure we align them quickly and in a unified direction.”
He calls Europe’s instinct to build everything itself “arrogant,” and says refusing a machine because it comes from the U.S. would be “politically stupid.” If Europe waits for its own hardware, he warns, “you will have another Microsoft that is not going to be in Europe, that is going to sell you the software.”

articles.title_orig: 400-year-old shipwreck lock finally opened after researchers crack secret code: 'Incredibly satisfying'
articles.title_zh: 400-year-old shipwreck lock finally opened after researchers crack secret code: 'Incredibly satisfying'
articles.content_orig:
Researchers in Wales used non-destructive CT scanning to peer inside a 400-year-old brass combination lock from the 1583 shipwreck of the Ann Francis, lining up internal notches to crack its four-letter code — ANCE — without damaging the artifact.
A 400-year-old brass lock recovered from a 16th-century shipwreck off the coast of Wales has finally been opened — and researchers didn't need a key to crack it.
The discovery, conducted as a joint effort between Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) and Cardiff University, was announced earlier this month.
Museum officials said in a statement that the brass lock had "remained firmly locked" since its vessel was destroyed off the coast of Wales in the 16th century.
DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS
The Ann Francis was overtaken by a storm on Dec. 28, 1583, while returning from Spain.
It was blown off course before wrecking on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot.
A centuries-old brass padlock from the wreck of the Ann Francis remained sealed for more than 400 years before experts identified its four-letter combination without damaging the artifact. (Amgueddfa Cymru/Museum Wales)
More than 400 years later, metal detectorist Peter Hughes began unearthing parts of the ship's hoard on Margam Beach in 1996.
He continued recovering artifacts from the site through 2017 — including the brass lock — after dredging and storms stripped away layers of sand.
Speaking to officials, Hughes said he was "immediately astonished" when he uncovered the lock.
TREASURE HUNTER STRIKES GOLD WITH 1,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY LINKED TO 'HAND OF GOD'
"When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief," he said, as Cardiff University reported.
"I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things [in] the treasure chest it once locked."
The Ann Francis was overtaken by a storm on Dec. 28, 1583, while returning from Spain and blown off course before wrecking on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot in Wales. Port Talbot is pictured above. (iStock)
Researchers revealed the four-letter combination that kept it sealed for more than four centuries: ANCE.
To crack the code without damaging the artifact, museum experts partnered with specialists at Cardiff University to examine the lock's internal mechanism using CT scanning technology.
"Now [that] we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."
'SPECTACULAR' SHIPWRECK FOUND WITH UNDERWATER TIME CAPSULE OF UNTOUCHED CARGO: 'AMAZING FIND'
David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said micro-CT scanning allowed him to inspect the interior of the lock without harming it.
"By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination," said Williams, according to Cardiff University.
Found near Spanish silver coins and two coin weights, the 16th-century padlock from the Ann Francis wreck is now on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea, Wales. (Amgueddfa Cymru/Museum Wales)
"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," he said.
After waiting until later that evening for museum officials to test the code, Williams got the news that it worked.
"Getting the message that we'd cracked it was incredibly satisfying," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Alastair Willis, a senior curator at Amgueddfa Cymru, said the meaning behind the lock's code remains unknown.
"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain , but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve," said Willis, the release noted.
He added, "Of course, now [that] we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."
Officials said the lock is believed to have once secured a small chest holding valuables.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Because it was found near Spanish silver coins and two coin weights, researchers think it may have protected those items or a chest containing organic materials that did not survive, such as documents or textiles.
The hoard also included rare gold coins dating to the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, as well as a boatswain's whistle.
Rare gold coins dating to the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain were also recovered from the Ann Francis treasure hoard. (Amgueddfa Cymru/Museum Wales)
The combination lock and other artifacts from the Ann Francis hoard are now on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Recent archaeological and historical finds across Wales have drawn similar attention.
Earlier this year, archaeologists revealed new findings from a remote Roman fort in Wales — including fourth-century coins and artifacts — that may link the site to a centuries-old legend about Emperor Magnus Maximus.

Last winter, volunteers cleaning a South Wales beach uncovered roughly 200 mysterious old-fashioned shoes that may have washed ashore from a 19th-century shipwreck.

articles.title_orig: Russia is escalating conflict in Europe and in space, warns Friedrich Merz
articles.title_zh: Russia is escalating conflict in Europe and in space, warns Friedrich Merz
articles.content_orig:
Keep reading for the latest news in Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, November 25:
Numerous sources inside Russian foreign policy circles on Wednesday underscored the Kremlin's desire for European diplomats to travel to Moscow and explain their intentions before they be allowed to participate in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn.
Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained."
Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations."
He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace.
Nechayev said the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are."
Russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve."
Poland 's Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told reporters that Warsaw will set up a no-fly zone inside its border with Ukraine and suggested other regional allies do the same in the wake of repeated Russian incursions into NATO airspace as part of Moscow's war of aggression.
"An ordinance is already being prepared by the government and should enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January," said Tomczyk.
"We will also urge our allies — the ⁠entire ​NATO alliance — to establish such a ​principle along the eastern flank," he continued, "Poland was a pioneer ​in this regard, ‌and the Baltic states have since followed our lead."
Poland strictly limits air traffic at its border already.
On Wednesday, Tomczyk said the proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory from the border and provide added support for Poland's armed forces.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended his government's expenditures on Ukraine aid during a budget debate in the Bundestag on Wednesday.
Merz tackled criticism from opposition parties on the left and right head on, saying "Russia knows exactly ​what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine."
"Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea. Russia ​is escalating ‌in space. And Russia is now escalating massively here, in our own country, too, even at the risk of loss of life," he added.
Merz said, "anyone who doesn't see that, doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims."
The Left Party and Alternative for Germany (AfD) have both called for an end to Ukraine aid and better relations with Moscow .
Among other things, Germany blames Russia for an explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport this summer as well as cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace incursions across the EU and NATO .
Merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself. "We are learning from Ukraine," said Merz, "technologically for civilian use but of course also in defense ⁠technology."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Kyiv and Moscow both assessed damage to energy infrastructure on Wednesday morning as both sides continued to inflict damage on one another amid Russia's over four-and-a-half-year attempted invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in .
Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations.
Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks.
In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts.
Kyiv's attacks on Russian ships in and off the coast of Libya over the past couple of days have ruffled feathers among Ukraine's allies, with France and Italy, for instance, coming down on entirely different sides of the issue.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday announced that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship.
Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot said, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity."
Barrot said Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?"
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions.
Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on ⁠Wednesday, Tajani said, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in ​Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port."
Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
As Russia's invasion of Ukraine creeps toward its fifth year, both sides continue to blast each other's infrastructure.
Overnight attacks targeted gas, oil and thermal energy facilities on both sides of the conflict's front lines.
While Moscow chided former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson's calls for a contingent of Western soldiers to be stationed in Ukraine, France's foreign minister defended Kyiv's recent attacks on Russian maritime vessels in far away Libya — something Italy's foreign minister criticized.
In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended German support for Ukraine as opposition parties with sympathies for Moscow complain it's too expensive.
Merz called out those wanting to curtail support as either "failing to grasp" the fact that "Russia wants more than Ukraine" or "pursuing entirely different aims with regard to our country's freedom, openness and liberalism."
Lastly, Poland's defense minister on Wednesday expressed astonishment over the fact that the US has not yet condemned or even reacted to repeated Russian drone and missile incursions into Polish airspace in recent days.
Stay tuned to DW for these stories and all the latest news on the conflict in Ukraine….

articles.title_orig: Microsoft declares “Code Red” after huge Outlook outage
articles.title_zh: Microsoft declares “Code Red” after huge Outlook outage
articles.content_orig:
(Photo by Gene Medi/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Tech giant Microsoft declared a "Code Red" alert recently, signaling an urgent effort to address the historic 24-hour outage that downed its core products between Nov. 12-13.
The outage , which brought down the majority of Microsoft's core products, "affected most" of Microsoft's users, according to the company's post-incident report. The company's total user base is between 420 million and 450 million people, according to financial disclosures.
"Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in an email to employees Friday obtained by Reuters .
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
The incident also marked the most customer-impacting event in Microsoft's history, Henderson told employees.
Microsoft blamed the outage on a previously undetected scalability defect within the Windows operating system .
SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS
"Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson wrote.
Microsoft employees exchanged over 11,000 messages during the crisis in an effort to diagnose the issue, Microsoft Corporate Vice President Amanda Silver told employees in a memo Monday.
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'
Silver also detailed the nature of the "Code Red" rapid response, explaining that the mobilization would involve five work streams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms.
She added that, in the event of a future situation of a similar nature, the company is working on a target to be able to restore service to users within one hour. The company will also work on deploying AI agents to help with quicker diagnosis in the future.
LAWMAKERS WARN AMERICANS OF VULNERABLE SYSTEMS AMID STREAK OF OUTAGES: 'SOMETHING IS GOING ON'
An estimate from the Anderson Economic Group approximated that the outage cost the global economy roughly $7 billion in lost productivity value.
Henderson, in another memo, told employees that urgent patches to Microsoft's flagship M365 suite took too long to deploy.
"In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.
Fox News Digital contacted Microsoft for further comment.

articles.title_orig: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
articles.title_zh: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: China space station receives Pakistani astronaut on 'historic mission'
articles.title_zh: China space station receives Pakistani astronaut on 'historic mission'
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

articles.content_orig:
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least five people, wounded dozens of others and caused power outages in five regions, local authorities said.
Deputy Energy ⁠Minister Artem Nekrasov said on Wednesday that the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, ‌Donetsk, Zaporizhia, Odesa and Kharkiv were affected.
He said the situation was difficult in Zaporizhia and Dnipropetrovsk, where the attacks damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply.
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant lost ⁠external power after ⁠shelling and ⁠switched to diesel generators, he said, noting that it was the unit’s 17th ‌loss of external power this year.
“Repair and restoration work is ongoing in all affected regions. At the same time, repeated enemy attacks and constant air raid alerts are significantly complicating these operations and delaying the restoration of electricity supply,” the Ministry of Energy said in a statement relayed by the Interfax news agency.
The outages come after ⁠Russian ⁠strikes killed two people and injured three others, including a ⁠child, in Ukraine’s Black Sea region of Odesa, hitting cars and ⁠private and industrial buildings, Governor Oleh Kiper said on Telegram late on Tuesday.
In northern Ukraine, Russian forces struck enterprises in the Chernihiv region late on Tuesday, killing one person, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) reported late on Tuesday.
In eastern Ukraine, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region seven times over the past day, killing one person in Kramatorsk, the head of Donetsk Regional Military Administration, Vadym Filashkin, said on Wednesday.
Russian forces also attacked Kharkiv city and six settlements in the region over the past day. One person was killed and 14 others were injured in the attacks, the head of Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, Oleh Syniehubov, said, according to Interfax.
Russian forces also attacked the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, with drones overnight, triggering a fire in a multistorey apartment building and injuring two people, the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said.
Meanwhile, in Russia, ⁠⁠a ⁠⁠Ukrainian drone attack killed one ⁠⁠person and triggered power ⁠⁠cuts in the Samara region, a ⁠⁠major ⁠⁠oil refining hub for the state oil company ‌‌Rosneft, Russian news agencies quoted Governor ⁠⁠Vyacheslav Fedorishchev as saying ⁠⁠on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: EU plans €50bn tech fund to close gap with US and China
articles.title_zh: EU plans €50bn tech fund to close gap with US and China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll , a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .
Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.
The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

articles.title_orig: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.title_zh: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.content_orig:
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.
Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.
Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around.
No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world.
According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source.
Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”
Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee.
Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled.
The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”
Jean Lee reports with NBC News’ Social Newsgathering team in Los Angeles. She previously reported for the NBC News investigative unit.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

Markets started the day on a weaker footing after a sell-off in semiconductor stocks, with Nvidia ( NVDA ) shares losing nearly 6% Tuesday and continuing to decline on Wednesday. The focus on Wednesday turns to the latest PCE data and whether it shifts bets on the Federal Reserve's expected December rate hike. articles.title_orig: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.title_zh: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine .
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.
Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.
“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.
It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”
Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.
During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

articles.title_orig: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.title_zh: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.content_orig:
Giorgia Meloni has a Ukraine problem.
With a national Italian election possible as early as this spring, Kyiv’s weekend strikes on a Russian warship and cargo vessel in Libya risk sparking a backlash in Rome — a Kyiv ally that also has traditionally close ties with the North African country.
“If this is a continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine just a few hundred kilometers from Italy, this is worrying, especially because we work for the stability of Libya,” said Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, who added that Rome had not been informed ahead of time about the attack.
The Italian foreign ministry said Tajani spoke with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday.
"The Minister reiterated to his Ukrainian counterpart how vital it is for Italy to continue working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading to the Mediterranean as well," the ministry said in a statement . For Italy, "it is essential to respect Libya’s sovereignty and to continue working towards the country’s stability, unity and sovereignty."
Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, a pro-Kremlin junior partner in Meloni’s governing coalition, that opposes further military aid to Ukraine said that “it wouldn't make sense” if military support provided to Ukraine “ends up making wars and sinking ships around the world.”
Kyiv defended its right to strike Russian vessels — even those docked in Benghazi, thousands of kilometers away from the battlefield.
The issue threatens to become a headache for Meloni.
Rome is especially concerned about destabilizing Libya, a former Italian colony, fearing that if the politically fragile country collapses into disorder again, it could spark a migration wave across the Mediterranean.
Russia and its allies in Libya could use migration as a weapon against the country, said Arturo Varvelli, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
“For Italy, Libya is the most important foreign policy dossier because everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy,” said Lia Quartapelle, a center-left Democratic Party lawmaker and vice chair of the Foreign and European Affairs Committee of Italy’s parliament.
Meloni's strong backing for Ukraine puts her at odds with part of her coalition, as well as with large parts of the political opposition.
This summer, former Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte, leader of the populist 5Star Movement, a key opposition party, set off a political firestorm by questioning further military aid to Ukraine if the center-left wins the next election.
The far-right opposition National Future Party, led by former Gen. Roberto Vannacci, also opposes military aid to Ukraine.
The public is also skeptical. Italians are the least likely to support Ukraine among major Western European countries, with a YouGov survey earlier this year finding that only 32% of Italians care if it wins against Russia.
For Meloni, "it’s a difficult match to handle," said pollster Lorenzo Pregliasco. "We [Italians] are afraid to take sides; we tend to be wary of conflict and of any Italian involvement in any conflict whatsoever."
That national caution has made Italy a relatively small donor to Ukraine — giving far less than countries like Germany or Nordic nations. Italy has provided around €3 billion in military aid, boosted by a new €800 million package.
Although there is worry about blowback, military giving "is unlikely to be affected in a meaningful way by the Ukrainian attacks," said Alessandro Marrone, who leads the defense, security and space program at Rome’s Istituto Affari Internazionali.
And it's not just Italy that is worried about a widening war in the Mediterranean.
“Greece’s government is concerned that the war in Ukraine could open another front in the eastern Mediterranean and is planning to have discussions on the issue with like-minded partners in the near future,” a senior Greek government official said.
Despite the turmoil in Rome and Athens, Kyiv stands by its decision to attack Russian ships.
“Ukraine is defending itself against the armed aggression of the Russian Federation. Our actions constitute the exercise of the inherent right to self-defense," Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters on Tuesday.
"Ukraine has the full right to strike the aggressor’s legitimate military targets. These include Russian warships, cargo vessels transporting military equipment and resources, and tankers belonging to the shadow fleet that sustain Russia’s war machine," he said. "Ukraine is not dragging anyone into the war, nor is it exporting the conflict elsewhere."
There is another risk for Meloni: that Ukraine ends up showing the lack of an Italian strategy in Libya to deal with the Russian presence there, said Varvelli, the ECFR researcher. The Russian naval vessel was sunk in the eastern Libyan port of Benghazi, controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army is allied with Moscow.
"The Ukrainians are simply bringing to light the significant Russian presence in Libya, which consists of six bases and between 1,000 and 1,500 personnel," he said, warning that Italy is “purely reactive” to what is happening in the country.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv and Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting from Athens.

articles.title_orig: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.title_zh: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.
